articles.title: Relationship expert explains why people ghost and what they may regret later
articles.summary: Relationship expert Monica Ricci shares why ghosting is a classic avoidance behavior and what it truly says about the person who disappears.
articles.body: If you've ever dated someone who stopped reaching out and responding to texts, without any conversation about ending the relationship, you’ve been ghosted. "Ghosting," or the sudden absence or unresponsiveness of a potential partner, is more than just feeling ignored by someone you’re interested in, according to Monica Ricci, a Georgia-based relationship coach — it's a complete disappearance without closure. Why do people ghost? Ricci suggested it’s a "classic avoidance behavior." "It's the same reason we procrastinate — we're avoiding some kind of discomfort," she said. THE MARRIAGE WARNING SIGN THAT MAY BE WORSE THAN FIGHTING — AND 4 WAYS TO TURN THINGS AROUND "It could be a fear of having a really hard conversation. It could be not wanting to disappoint a person," Ricci went on. "Someone could ghost because they just don't care enough. They're just not invested enough that they believe it [would] warrant communicating to say, ‘Hey, this isn't working for me.'" Those who do the ghosting may feel a sudden sense of relief, according to Ricci, but may also have lingering guilt around how the relationship was left unfinished. A new paper based on three studies, published in Sage Journals, suggests people who are ghosted underestimate the guilt and remorse felt by those who cut off contact. 5 MARRIAGE MISTAKES COUPLES MAKE WITHOUT REALIZING IT — AND HOW TO AVOID THEM "There's a part of you that may know that wasn't the best way to handle it," Ricci said. "And so it may stay with you a lot longer because it calls into question the kind of person you want to be." It’s easy to take ghosting personally, she noted. "But the truth is, if you're being ghosted, it says more about the person who ghosted you and their ability to have honest communication, their ability to step up in an uncomfortable situation and really choose their behavior over their discomfort." After a ghosting, the brain will automatically begin searching for patterns and answers to "make things make sense," Ricci said. WHY COUPLES SHOULD FLIRT WITH EACH OTHER EVERY DAY — PLUS THE ‘RED FLAG’ TO AVOID At some point, moving forward means accepting that you may never get an explanation and recognizing that being ghosted is not a reflection of your worth, according to the expert. "If a person can't have a conversation with you at the beginning of a relationship that is honest and frank, they probably weren't your person anyway," she added. How to communicate honestly Ricci, whose expertise is based on the Gottman Method — an approach to couples therapy focused on building emotional intimacy, improving communication and managing conflict — said seemingly difficult conversations can be easier than people expect. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "When you want to communicate that this dating relationship is not a good fit anymore, it's easiest to be very direct and brief," she said. This can be as simple as sending a text saying, "I have enjoyed getting to know you. I'm not feeling the kind of connection that I need to move forward, and I wish you all the best in finding a great match." "If a person can't have a conversation with you at the beginning of a relationship that is honest and frank, they probably weren't your person anyway." "You're honest, you're truthful, you're not making it about them being a bad person," she said. "You're saying, ‘I'm just not feeling the kind of connection I need to move forward.'" CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Although being forthright is the respectful option, it's not possible to control how the other person will feel or react, Ricci noted. "And this is sometimes where the ghosting comes from – we don't want to make someone feel bad," she said. "It’s this illusion that we have some control over how a person feels … But the reality is the least painful and kindest option is to just be direct." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ However, in a situation where you are being harassed, stalked or abused, ghosting may be the safest option, Ricci emphasized. "If someone is treating you really poorly, or harassing you, or stalking you … ghosting is absolutely the most appropriate," she said. "Cutting a person off completely, not responding, is the safest, smartest way to go."

articles.title: Son sounds alarm after father's medically assisted death in Canada: Way past appropriate'
articles.summary: Eric Edmeades says Canada's MAiD program moved so fast his father died before the family could prepare, warning safeguards have gone too far.
articles.body: A Canadian man's decision to end his life through the country's medically assisted dying program left his son stunned by how quickly the process unfolded, and now he's warning that the system has gone "way past appropriate." Eric Edmeades, founder of Speaker Nation, a training platform for speakers that teaches presentation skills and more, told Fox News Digital this week that his father Baz, who was in his late 70s and struggling with a combination of medical problems, began discussing Canada's Medical Assistance in Dying (MAiD) program after his health deteriorated in late 2023. But what Edmeades expected to be a months-long process suddenly accelerated, leaving the family with little time to prepare. I'M 25 WITH A TERMINAL DISEASE. WE NEED AN FDA COMMISSIONER THAT HEARS PEOPLE LIKE ME Edmeades said the family started taking the issue seriously in January, but at that stage, projections were that it would take at least six months. He and his wife traveled to Vancouver at the beginning of 2024 to visit his father. At that stage, it was still a speculative thing that was months away. "And then all of a sudden it was like, ‘No, it's next week,’" Edmeades recalled. His father died via MAiD on Feb. 27, 2024. He had been experiencing a sharp decline in his physical health and independence, particularly during the COVID-era lockdowns, according to his son. "He had been incredibly healthy most of his life," Edmeades said, describing a combination of symptoms that included epilepsy and neurological pain. Edmeades also questioned whether interactions between his father's medications could have contributed to his deteriorating condition. "When the lockdowns came along, and he could no longer go out and walk all the time, it really had a marked decrease in his physical ability and his sense of freedom and all that kind of stuff," he said. "And then there just came this point where life started sounding pointless to him," Edmeades said. CATHOLIC NUNS SUE NEW YORK, SAY ASSISTED SUICIDE LAW FORCES THEM TO VIOLATE THEIR FAITH Edmeades said his father had previously spoken about suicide, making his initial interest in medically assisted dying less surprising to the family. "Given that it wasn't the first time that he talked about suicide in his life, it wasn't particularly shocking, but he also wasn't talking about it in really alarmist terms. So, I wasn't overly worried about it," he said. Edmeades and his wife had already planned a trip to Vancouver and were able to spend time with his father before his death. "And one of the things I'm incredibly grateful for is that I had incidentally booked a trip out to Vancouver, and my wife and I got to spend time with him," Edmeades recalled. He thought he and and his wife would have another opportunity to visit. NEW YORK NUNS' CHALLENGE TO ASSISTED SUICIDE LAW IS ABOUT PROTECTING FREEDOM, LAWYER SAYS Edmeades said he was not in contact with his father's medical providers at the time and did not fully understand what had happened until afterward. "It happened so quickly that I only really started to piece together what happened when it was done," he said. Other family members and friends had also expressed concerns about his father's decision, according to Edmeades. He recalled that his brother openly opposed the decision and that one of his father's close friends spent approximately 45 minutes discussing the matter with him during his final days. "At that stage, you know, for him, the decision was made," Edmeades said. The experience has left Edmeades questioning whether Canada's assisted-dying program has adequate safeguards. He acknowledged that there may be circumstances in which medically assisted dying is appropriate but argued that Canada's implementation has gone too far. "What I see happening in Canada is way past appropriate," he said. Edmeades also raised concerns about the government's role in overseeing the system, arguing that decisions about eligibility should be insulated from political influence and potential financial incentives. "If I had to press a button and decide whether the MAiD program existed or didn't exist, I would say this," Edmeades said. "It should only ever exist if, and I mean if the process for approving people, it would be completely independent of government, and there could be no benefit to those people in making that preference in making that decision. Because otherwise there's a slippery slope, and we see that slippery slope." According to the Government of Canada, individuals seeking medical assistance in dying (MAiD) must be at least 18 years old, capable of making their own medical decisions, and eligible for publicly funded healthcare. They must also voluntarily request the procedure without outside pressure and provide informed consent. To qualify, applicants must have a serious, incurable illness, disease or disability, be experiencing an advanced and irreversible decline in their abilities, and face persistent physical or psychological suffering they consider intolerable and that cannot be relieved in a way they find acceptable. The government also announced legislation on Oct. 27, 2026, that would allow advance requests while preventing the planned expansion of MAiD eligibility to people whose sole underlying medical condition is mental illness. According to the BBC, Canada’s MAiD law, which legalized euthanasia in 2016, is responsible for one in every 20 deaths in Canada. NEW YORK NUNS WILL NOT BE FORCED TO COMPLY WITH ASSISTED-SUICIDE LAW WHILE CASE PROGRESSES A report from the Canadian Medical Association Journal covered by EWTN News claimed that implementing assisted suicide will "save" the Canadian healthcare system between $34.7 and $136.8 million per year. The study noted that patients and physicians should not consider costs when making such grave decisions. In a statement to Fox News Digital, Ian McLeod, senior advisor for media relations and Conseiller principal for the Department of Justice Canada, said, "Canadian law is extremely clear: medical assistance in dying (MAID) requires a voluntary request, freedom from external pressure, and the person’s informed consent, among other stringent eligibility criteria and safeguards. Knowingly failing to comply with these eligibility criteria and safeguards is a criminal offence." McLeod continued, "In the current MAID structure found in Canada’s Criminal Code, the mental illness exclusion is meant to exclude eligibility for MAID on the basis of a mental illness, including suicidal ideation. The proposed amendment to the mental illness exclusion in Bill C-41, the proposed Medical Assistance in Dying Safeguards Act, which was introduced on October 27, 2026, is meant to reinforce this." McLeod added, "This is why the Bill reinforces that, in situations where a person has a mental illness and an eligible medical condition (e.g. physical or neurodegenerative illness), eligibility must be determined on the basis of the qualifying medical condition. A mental illness may contribute to a person’s suffering, but it cannot be the basis for determining that the MAID eligibility criteria are met. Importantly, having a mental illness does not, in itself, make a person ineligible for MAID." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP McLeod said that patients whose natural deaths are not reasonably foreseeable must undergo eligibility assessments by two independent doctors or nurse practitioners, with at least 90 full days between the start of the first assessment and the assisted death. That waiting period, according to McLeod, can be shortened if both assessments are complete, both practitioners agree the patient is at imminent risk of losing the ability to consent, and the practitioner providing MAiD determines that a shorter period is appropriate. McLeod emphasized that federal requirements establish minimum safeguards, while provinces and territories oversee how MAiD is administered and may impose additional protections. He said questions about the program's oversight and delivery should therefore be directed to provincial or territorial authorities.

articles.title: Dinner dispute turns fatal; wife stabs ex-Army man to death in Ahmedabad
articles.summary: Ahmedabad Naroda: Woman allegedly stabs retired Army man husband to death after dinner dispute; accused Nirmala Kharadi arrested within hours, murder case filed.
articles.body: Ahmedabad: What began as a minor dinner-time argument in Naroda ended in tragedy when a 34-year-old woman allegedly plunged a kitchen knife into her husband’s chest during a heated dispute over the meal prepared at home. The victim, 39-year-old retired Army serviceman and GMDC contractual driver Dilipbhai Kharadi, succumbed to his injuries at a hospital, turning a domestic quarrel into a murder case.Police arrested the accused, identified as Nirmala Kharadi, and booked her for murder. The murder has left the couple’s two children without their father, while their mother remains in police custody.According to Naroda PI B M Katariya, Nirmala stabbed Dilip Kharadi on the left side of his chest after a heated argument at their residence in Naroda Smart City-2 around midnight on Thursday. “The couple had reportedly been quarrelling frequently over domestic and financial issues for nearly a year, and the latest dispute allegedly erupted over the dinner prepared that night,” he said.The PI said the accused will now be questioned to determine what led to the fatal quarrel. According to police, the couple had been facing minor domestic disputes for some time. On Thursday, an argument escalated when the wife allegedly responded angrily, leading to a heated exchange in which both parties abused each other. The confrontation eventually culminated in the stabbing, police said.According to the complaint filed by Dilip’s father, 73-year-old Somaji Kharadi, a retired unarmed ASI of Rajkot city police, the couple often argued over household matters, including what food should be cooked. On Thursday night, another disagreement broke out, during which Nirmala allegedly lost her temper, picked up a kitchen knife and attacked her husband.The murder came to light after Nirmala allegedly called her brother-in-law, Mukesh, around midnight and informed him that she had stabbed Dilip in the chest during an argument. She allegedly told him that her husband had become unconscious and that she was taking him to Shalby Hospital.On Friday afternoon, Mukesh informed his father that Dilip had been injured in a quarrel and admitted to hospital. Somaji, accompanied by family members, rushed to the hospital but was informed by doctors that his son had succumbed to his injuries.The complainant stated that he noticed a stab wound on the left side of Dilip’s chest, along with injuries on his right cheek, right upper arm, and near the thumbs of both hands. He also said the family had initially withheld news of the death from him to spare him the shock. Dilip retired from the Army in 2022.Naroda police formed multiple teams and analysed CCTV footage while gathering local intelligence to trace the accused. Nirmala was arrested within hours of the crime. Police registered a case of murder along with offences under the Gujarat Police Act and are continuing their investigation.The PI said that the dispute erupted after the husband asked why she had cooked a particular vegetable and this was countered by the wife, which eventually ended up with both the husband and wife abusing each other. articles.title: Pro-trans activists hold rally against Washington state ballot initiative to protect girls sports
articles.summary: Protesters marched through Seattle Thursday after Washington voters approved Initiative 638 barring biological males from girls' K-12 sports.
articles.body: Transgender-rights supporters marched through downtown Seattle Thursday after Washington voters approved a measure barring biological males from girls’ K–12 interscholastic sports, setting up a potential court battle over the new restrictions. Demonstrators gathered at Westlake Park before marching toward Pike Place Market, according to KUOW. The protest followed the passage of Initiative 638, which also requires students seeking to compete in girls’ sports to provide medical verification of their biological sex. The measure had 56.8% support in returns reported Thursday by FOX 13 Seattle. The Associated Press called its passage Wednesday evening, with ballots still being counted. WASHINGTON STATE VOTERS APPEAR TO PASS FIRST-EVER BALLOT MEASURE SEPARATING BOYS AND GIRLS SPORTS "I was kind of expecting it, but it was still devastating nonetheless," Evan Gortner of Gender Equity Movement, which organized the protest, told KUOW. Marchers chanted, "638 is trans hate." Some attendees also criticized Democratic leaders for not doing more to defeat the initiative. The result delivered a victory to Let’s Go Washington, the conservative group behind the measure, even as voters rejected two other initiatives it backed concerning parental rights and the repeal of the state’s tax on high earners. Supporters argue that separating girls’ sports by biological sex protects fairness, safety and athletic opportunities for female students. Opponents contend the restrictions discriminate against transgender students and could subject girls to intrusive medical verification. WOMEN WHO FACED BIOLOGICAL MALES IN GIRLS' SPORTS AND LOCKER ROOMS SPEAK OUT AHEAD OF WASHINGTON STATE VOTE The dispute now extends beyond the election results. Gender Justice League Executive Director Danni Askini told KUOW her organization was consulting partners and evaluating a possible challenge on student-privacy grounds. The group had not formally announced a lawsuit in that Nov. 5 report. The ACLU of Washington also condemned the outcome, but told KUOW it does not discuss potential litigation. That response did not announce a lawsuit. Washington Democrats, meanwhile, have said they support other organizations pursuing challenges but will not bring a case themselves. "WA Dems will not be challenging the initiative in court. We believe there will be organizations who do and we support those efforts," the party previously told OutKick. Party Chair Shasti Conrad called the initiative unconstitutional in a Nov. 5 statement. The measure’s medical-verification requirement has become a central point of contention. Its text requires a health examination and consent form, or another statement signed by a student’s personal healthcare provider, verifying biological sex as part of the required routine sports physical. That verification must rely on reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup or naturally produced testosterone levels. The text does not prescribe a particular examination or test. Washington has allowed students to compete on teams consistent with their gender identity since 2007. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The debate also prompted protests from female athletes before the election. About a dozen Camas girls declined to race against a transgender teammate on Oct. 13, OutKick previously reported. For schools, the immediate question is how to carry out the new requirements. The Washington Interscholastic Activities Association told KUOW it was preparing changes for Dec. 3 and reviewing implementation, including physical-examination requirements. It said updated guidance and forms would go to schools after legal review.

articles.title: Certain sleep habits could offer clues to hidden type of depression, scientists say
articles.summary: A study of over 11,000 Australian adults links specific sleep habits and circadian rhythm disruptions to a newly proposed subtype of depression.
articles.body: A person's sleep habits may help identify a newly proposed subtype of depression linked to the body's internal clock. In a study of 11,380 Australian adults with a history of depression, about 23% met researchers' criteria for what they called "circadian depression." The profile included at least three of six features: being an evening person, waking up feeling very tired, sleeping longer during the worst periods of depression, experiencing seasonal changes, having a later midpoint between falling asleep and waking up, and experiencing "social jetlag," a large shift in sleep timing between workdays and days off. The seasonal changes could involve sleep, mood, activity, appetite, weight or energy. THE DAYTIME HABIT THAT COULD TRANSFORM YOUR SLEEP, ACCORDING TO NEW STUDY The study, published on Oct. 20 in The British Journal of Psychiatry, could eventually help guide more personalized care for patients with depression, according to the researchers. "Depression is not a uniform illness, and understanding the characteristics of different subtypes means we can give people earlier access to treatments that will be most effective for them," first author Emiliana Tonini, Ph.D., from the University of Sydney's Brain and Mind Centre, said in a statement. The label, however, is not a formal diagnosis and needs independent replication and further study, the researchers noted. Treatment questions People in the circadian group reported an earlier onset of depression and more severe symptoms than those who did not meet the criteria. They were also more likely to report weight gain during depressive episodes. They also reported poorer responses and more side effects with two common classes of antidepressants, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs). POPULAR SLEEP AIDS BEFORE SURGERY COULD PREVENT PAINKILLER DEPENDENCE LATER Participants reported how well their medications worked, but the study did not explain why some were less effective and did not test treatments aimed at adjusting the body’s internal clock. Researchers said light exposure, regular sleep schedules and melatonin-related approaches warrant further study. Dr. Ian Hickie, a study co-author and professor of psychiatry at the University of Sydney, said the proposed profile "cuts across existing historic subtypes" of depression, most commonly atypical and bipolar depression, because they share features such as low energy and oversleeping. COMMON GYM SUPPLEMENT COULD HELP FIGHT DEPRESSION, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS Atypical depression can also involve weight gain, while bipolar depression refers to depressive episodes in people with bipolar disorder, which also involves periods of unusually elevated or irritable mood and increased energy. "We define circadian only by sleep-wake and circadian features," Hickie told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES For some people with this profile, Hickie said sleep-wake disruption may be more than a symptom of depression. "This type of circadian disturbance is not simply a consequence, but the underlying cause," he wrote. The study itself, however, could not establish whether body-clock disruption caused depression or resulted from it. Staying up late or having trouble waking does not necessarily indicate depression. Participants had already reported depression, which in some cases was severe, recurring or long-lasting. Participants in the circadian group also reported more manic-like experiences. John Puls, a psychotherapist and adjunct professor at Florida Atlantic University, said those symptoms could help explain their reported response to antidepressants. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "SSRIs are not meant to treat these more significant mental health symptoms that go far beyond depressive symptoms," Puls, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital. "In fact, some SSRIs can actually worsen manic symptoms, which lead to poor sleep." Study limitations There were several limitations to the study, the researchers acknowledged. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Participants reported their own sleep patterns and treatment experiences, and the cross-sectional analysis didn't show whether sleep disruption preceded or followed depressive symptoms. All participants were of European ancestry, so the findings may not apply to other populations. Jillian Amodio, a Maryland-based psychotherapist and founder of Moms For Mental Health, cautioned against using the findings as "a benchmark for treating each person in the same way." "Biological, environmental, social and psychological factors all need to be accounted for," Amodio, who was not involved in the research, told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Researchers should examine more populations, including people who work night shifts, and account for differences in time zones and seasons, according to Amodio. The study was led by researchers at the University of Sydney and QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute, with co-authors from institutions in Australia, the U.K. and the U.S.

articles.title: Swansea mum tries to raise £2.95m for son's dementia treatment
articles.summary: The dementia treatment for children is available in the US, with funding for UK children unclear.
articles.body:
The mum of a five-year-old boy with a rare form of dementia has to pay almost £3m for his life saving treatment.

Tate McDaid, from Swansea, was diagnosed with Sanfilippo Syndrome - a form of dementia that just over 100 UK children have - when he was four .

In September, the first gene therapy to treat the condition in children was approved in the US.

His mum Tammy said she spent "months praying" for its approval but discovered the treatment is to set cost £2.95 million per child, with it unclear how families outside the US can fund this.

Health officials from Wales are currently talking to those in the US to see what potential access pathways there are for Tate.

"I was excited when the treatment initially got approved but then reality hit hard the next day," Tammy said.

This was when she read the US price for the one-time treatment had been set at $3.95 million.

Tammy contacted Ultragenyx, who developed the treatment, in the hope of understanding how families outside the US, who do not have health insurance there, will cover the costs.

"We understand what they are charging for American citizens, but they've got health insurance," she added.

"Not even just the UK, but everyone else in the world looking for this treatment."

Explaining how the US approved drug, FAYUVI, would work for families outside the US, Ultragenyx said: "There is not a single estimate we can provide for the total cost of care for an international patient, as those costs would depend on the patient's individual medical needs and the treating institution."

The Society for Mucopolysaccharide Diseases , a charity which helps children living with Sanfilippo Syndrome, said about 140 children in the UK have the condition.

There is currently no cure for Sanfilippo Syndrome Type A, also called Mucopolysaccharidosis type III (MPS III), but the new drug could delay its onset, and allow Tate to remain active for longer.

The condition, described as "childhood Alzheimer's" or "childhood dementia" due to its neurodegenerative nature, causes the gradual loss of abilities, such as walking and eating.

It can progress more rapidly after the age of five, which is why Tammy said "it's really a battle of time" for her to raise enough money to get her son the treatment that is not available yet in the UK.

She said: "If a millionaire turned around tomorrow and gave us the money, we'd go to the US straight away."

With Tate turning six this month, Tammy doesn't believe time is on their side.

"Tate is already shown signs of cognitive decline," she added.

"The older he gets the less the treatment will work and the more ability he will lose in the process.

"I feel like we are at a turning point and I'm petrified."

Describing him as "the happiest little man" who is "blissfully unaware" of his problems, Tammy explained how important Tate's mobility is to him.

"He doesn't speak, he's never spoken. But his mobility is everything to him and that is why I'm fighting for it," she said.

Tammy began raising money before the new drug was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration and now has more than £160,000.

But this covers only about 5% of the total estimated cost of the treatment.

"Unfortunately, we're in a world where we need millions, not hundreds of thousands," she added.

"I'm just really hoping by some miracle the pharmaceutical company eventually come back to us and say they can do it for a little bit cheaper, but it's still going to be in the millions."

Ultragenyx said: "We are pursuing a global regulatory strategy, and FDA approval is an important first step in our long-term goal of bringing this treatment option to families around the world.

"We also understand the urgency families affected by Sanfilippo syndrome Type A face in identifying treatment options and why some may consider travelling to the US to access gene therapy.

"We recommend families work with their child's healthcare provider to understand what potential access pathways may exist before assuming this is their only option."

Staff from the Noah's Ark Children's Hospital in Cardiff are currently discussing this with officials in the US on the family's behalf.

articles.title: Simple bedtime change may help some individuals lose weight, study finds
articles.summary: An NYU clinical trial found that moving bedtime just one hour earlier led to weight loss in prediabetes patients, even without longer sleep.
articles.body: Falling asleep earlier was linked to greater weight loss in adults with prediabetes, according to new research. An analysis of data from a randomized trial led by the NYU Rory Meyers College of Nursing found that each hour earlier participants fell asleep was associated with roughly 1. 3 pounds of weight loss over eight weeks, although the finding does not prove that moving bedtime earlier causes weight loss. "When we fall asleep — not just how much we sleep — seems to be an important and overlooked factor for weight loss and metabolic health," Susan Kohl Malone, an assistant professor at the nursing college and the study's lead author, said in a press release. POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY PREVENT PREDIABETES FROM TURNING INTO DIABETES The investigation, published in the journal Nursing Research, evaluated 196 adults diagnosed with prediabetes who routinely logged fewer than 6.5 hours of sleep nightly. Half the group took part in an eight-week lifestyle education course on diet, exercise and stress. The other half received the same training alongside behavioral coaching meant to get them to go to bed earlier in gradual phases. DIETITIAN REVEALS SIMPLE EATING STRATEGY FOR BETTER SLEEP — AND ONE HABIT TO AVOID Researchers tracked participants’ blood sugar, sleep and activity using sensors, sleep logs and wrist-worn monitors. Neither group showed significant improvements in blood sugar. Both groups lost weight, but those receiving sleep coaching did not lose significantly more than those receiving lifestyle education alone. "While we expected that extending sleep would improve glucose levels and weight loss in adults with prediabetes who sleep for shorter periods, this wasn't the case in our study," Malone said. Participants who received sleep coaching did report better sleep quality and less daytime drowsiness, and they gradually began going to bed earlier. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER In a separate analysis across both groups, participants who shifted their sleep earlier tended to lose more weight. The researchers suggested the body’s internal clock may help explain the findings. Staying up late can increase exposure to artificial light, which may activate the body’s stress response and affect hormones that regulate hunger. Remaining awake late also coincides with the hours when human insulin sensitivity is at its lowest. "In contrast, falling asleep earlier may limit late-night eating and better align food intake with the body's optimal metabolic window," Malone noted. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES The trial ran for only eight weeks, which means it's unclear whether participants could maintain earlier bedtimes or sustain weight loss over the long term. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ While participants wore wrist monitors, key sleep metrics like rest quality and daytime drowsiness relied heavily on self-reported logs. The findings also show an association across the study group rather than proven cause and effect. Participants receiving sleep coaching fell asleep about 12 minutes earlier on average, according to Malone, which produced no measurable improvement in blood sugar levels.
